question: Implement Two Sum: given a slice of ints and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target, using a map for O(n) time.
thoughtProcess: The brute-force double loop is O(n^2). The classic optimization is a single pass with a map from value to index: for each number I check whether its complement, target minus the number, has already been seen. If so I have the answer; if not I record the current number and index and continue. This is O(n) because each lookup and insert is average O(1).
lineByLine: seen maps a previously visited value to its index, preallocated to len(nums) to avoid rehashing. The range loop walks each number with its index i. For each n I look up target-n, the complement that would complete the pair; if it was seen earlier at index j I return both indices in order. Otherwise I store n at index i so later numbers can find it. Returning nil signals no pair was found.
timeComplexity: O(n) — single pass, average O(1) map operations per element.
spaceComplexity: O(n) — the map can hold up to n entries.

alternativeApproaches.title: Brute force double loop
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Check every pair (i, j) with nested loops. Simple and uses O(1) extra space, but O(n^2) time, which is too slow for large inputs.

alternativeApproaches.title: Sort then two pointers
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Sort the values and converge two pointers from both ends. O(n log n) time and returns the values easily, but you lose the original indices unless you sort index pairs, so it is less natural when indices are required.

followUps.question: How would you handle the input containing duplicate values?
followUps.answer: The map approach handles duplicates correctly because it checks the complement before inserting the current element, so a pair like two equal numbers summing to the target is found when the second one looks up the first. If you stored everything first and then looked up, a value could match itself; checking-then-inserting avoids that. If multiple valid pairs exist and you need all of them, you would collect results in a slice instead of returning on the first match, and use a map from value to a list of indices.

followUps.question: Why preallocate the map with make(map[int]int, len(nums))?
followUps.answer: Giving make a size hint lets the runtime allocate enough buckets up front, so the map avoids repeated growth and rehashing as elements are inserted during the pass. It does not change the asymptotic complexity, which stays O(n), but it reduces constant-factor overhead and allocation churn for large inputs. It is a small idiomatic optimization that signals awareness of how Go maps grow, and it is harmless when the final size is smaller than the hint.

question: Reverse a singly linked list in place and return the new head.
thoughtProcess: Reversing a singly linked list iteratively means walking the list once while re-pointing each node's Next to its predecessor. I keep three references: prev (the already-reversed portion's head), curr (the node being processed), and a temporary next to remember the rest before I overwrite curr.Next. When curr becomes nil, prev is the new head. This is O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
lineByLine: prev starts nil because the reversed list is initially empty. curr begins at head. Each iteration saves next so we do not lose the rest of the list, then re-points curr.Next backward to prev, advances prev to curr, and advances curr to the saved next. When curr is nil the loop ends and prev points at what was the last node, now the head of the reversed list.
timeComplexity: O(n) — each node is visited exactly once.
spaceComplexity: O(1) — only three pointers regardless of list length.

alternativeApproaches.title: Recursive reversal
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Recurse to the end, then re-point each node on the way back. Elegant but uses O(n) stack space and risks a stack overflow on very long lists.

alternativeApproaches.title: Push onto a stack
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Push all nodes onto a stack, then pop to rebuild links in reverse order. Works but uses O(n) extra space and is more code than the in-place pointer rewiring.

followUps.question: Why is the iterative version preferred over the recursive one in production?
followUps.answer: The iterative version uses O(1) extra space because it only holds three pointers, while the recursive version uses O(n) stack frames, one per node. For a very long list the recursion can exhaust the goroutine stack and panic, whereas the iterative loop runs in constant space regardless of length. Go does not guarantee tail-call optimization, so the recursion's stack usage is real. The iterative approach is therefore the safer default for unbounded input sizes.

followUps.question: How would you reverse only the first k nodes?
followUps.answer: You run the same pointer-rewiring loop but stop after k iterations, keeping a reference to the original head, which becomes the tail of the reversed segment. After reversing k nodes, prev is the new head of that segment and curr points at the (k+1)th node, so you connect the original head's Next to curr to splice the unreversed remainder back on. This is the building block of reverse-in-k-groups, and the edge cases are when the list has fewer than k nodes, where you either leave it as is or reverse what remains depending on the spec.

question: Implement an LRU cache with O(1) Get and Put using container/list and a map.
thoughtProcess: An LRU cache needs O(1) access by key and O(1) reordering to mark an item most-recently-used. A map gives O(1) key lookup, and a doubly linked list gives O(1) move-to-front and remove-from-back. I store list elements in the map so I can find a node by key, move it to the front on access, and evict from the back when over capacity. Go's container/list is a ready-made doubly linked list, so I use it rather than hand-rolling pointers.
lineByLine: entry holds both key and value so eviction can find the key to delete from the map. LRUCache pairs a doubly linked list ll with a map items from key to its list element. Get looks up the element, and on a hit moves it to the front (most recent) and returns its value. Put updates and promotes an existing key, or pushes a new entry to the front and records it; if the list now exceeds capacity it evicts. evict removes the back element, the least recently used, from both the list and the map, using the stored key.
timeComplexity: O(1) for both Get and Put — map lookup plus constant-time list splicing.
spaceComplexity: O(capacity) — at most capacity entries in the map and list.

alternativeApproaches.title: Hand-rolled doubly linked list
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Define your own node with prev and next pointers instead of container/list. Avoids the interface type assertions and gives slightly better performance, at the cost of more code and manual pointer bookkeeping.

alternativeApproaches.title: Map with timestamps
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Store a last-used timestamp per key and scan for the oldest on eviction. Simple to write but eviction becomes O(n), so it fails the O(1) requirement and only suits small caches.

followUps.question: How would you make this cache safe for concurrent use?
followUps.answer: Wrap the cache in a sync.Mutex and lock it around the entire Get and Put bodies, because both methods mutate shared state: Get reorders the list, so even a read promotes an item and must be synchronized. A sync.RWMutex does not help much here since Get also writes by moving to front, unless you separate the read of the value from the promotion. For higher throughput you would shard the cache into multiple independently locked segments keyed by a hash, reducing contention, which is how production LRU caches like sharded designs scale.

followUps.question: Why store the key inside the entry as well as using it as the map key?
followUps.answer: When you evict the least-recently-used item you start from the back of the list, which gives you a list element but not directly the map key for that element. To delete the corresponding map entry you need the key, so storing it in the entry struct lets you recover it from the list node in O(1). Without it, you would have to scan the map to find which key points to that element, which is O(n) and defeats the constant-time guarantee. It is a small redundancy that keeps eviction O(1).

question: Build a worker pool that processes a list of integers concurrently and returns their sum, using channels and a WaitGroup.
thoughtProcess: A worker pool bounds concurrency to a fixed number of goroutines pulling from a shared jobs channel, which is better than spawning one goroutine per item. I send each number to a buffered jobs channel, start N workers that range over it, and have each worker send its partial result to a results channel. A WaitGroup tracks when all workers finish so I can close results, then I sum the results. The pool decouples the amount of work from the number of goroutines.
lineByLine: jobs carries the numbers, buffered to hold them all; results carries each worker's partial sum, buffered to the worker count. The loop starts N workers, each adding to the WaitGroup, ranging over jobs to accumulate a local sum, and sending that local sum once jobs is drained, then signaling Done. The main goroutine feeds all numbers into jobs and closes it so the range loops terminate. A separate goroutine waits for all workers and closes results, which lets the final range over results end naturally; total accumulates the partial sums.
timeComplexity: O(n) total work split across workers — wall-clock roughly O(n / workers) plus overhead.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the jobs buffer plus O(workers) for results and goroutines.

alternativeApproaches.title: Atomic accumulator
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Have workers add directly to a shared total with atomic.AddInt64 instead of sending partial sums. Avoids the results channel but introduces contention on the shared counter, which can be slower than per-worker local sums.

alternativeApproaches.title: errgroup for error handling
alternativeApproaches.explanation: If the work could fail, golang.org/x/sync/errgroup gives a pool that propagates the first error and cancels the rest via a shared context, which a plain WaitGroup does not do.

followUps.question: Why close the results channel from a separate goroutine after wg.Wait()?
followUps.answer: The main goroutine is busy ranging over results to collect the sums, so it cannot also block on wg.Wait() at the same time. Putting wg.Wait() and close(results) in their own goroutine lets the workers finish and the channel get closed concurrently while main drains results. Closing results is what makes the final range loop terminate. If you closed results before all workers had sent, a worker would panic sending on a closed channel; if you never closed it, the range loop would deadlock waiting forever.

followUps.question: Why have each worker keep a local sum instead of adding to a shared total?
followUps.answer: A per-worker local variable needs no synchronization because only that goroutine touches it, so the workers run without contending on a shared memory location. Each worker sends one final partial sum over the channel, and the single collecting goroutine combines them, so synchronization happens once per worker rather than once per number. Sharing a single counter would require atomic operations or a mutex on every addition, creating cache-line contention that can dominate runtime when many workers hammer the same address. Local accumulation plus a final reduce is the more scalable pattern.

question: Implement fan-in: merge several input channels into a single output channel.
thoughtProcess: Fan-in multiplexes many channels into one. I start a goroutine per input channel that copies every value into a shared output channel, and a WaitGroup tracks when all of them have drained their input. Once all inputs are exhausted I close the output so consumers know it is done. The key correctness points are closing output exactly once after all copiers finish, and using a WaitGroup rather than guessing when inputs are done.
lineByLine: out is the merged output channel. The WaitGroup is sized to the number of inputs. For each input channel a goroutine ranges over it, forwarding every value to out, and calls Done when its input closes; the channel is passed as an argument c to capture it correctly per iteration. A final goroutine waits for all copiers to finish, then closes out so downstream range loops terminate. The function returns out immediately as a receive-only channel while the goroutines run in the background.
timeComplexity: O(total values) forwarded across all inputs.
spaceComplexity: O(number of input channels) goroutines plus the channel buffers.

alternativeApproaches.title: Single goroutine with reflect.Select
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Use reflect.Select over a dynamic set of cases to read from all channels in one goroutine. Avoids per-channel goroutines but is slower and far less readable, so the goroutine-per-channel pattern is usually preferred.

alternativeApproaches.title: Fan-in with context cancellation
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Add a context so the merge can stop early if the consumer cancels, having each copier select on ctx.Done as well as the input, preventing goroutine leaks when the consumer abandons the output.

followUps.question: Why pass the channel as an argument to the goroutine instead of closing over the loop variable?
followUps.answer: In older Go versions the loop variable ch was shared across iterations, so a goroutine that closed over it could observe a later value once the loop advanced, causing all goroutines to read the same channel. Passing ch as the argument c captures the value at goroutine-creation time, giving each goroutine its own correct channel. As of Go 1.22 the loop variable is per-iteration so the bug no longer occurs, but passing the argument is still a clear, version-independent habit that makes the capture explicit.

followUps.question: What goroutine leak can fan-in cause and how do you prevent it?
followUps.answer: If the consumer stops reading from out before the inputs are drained, the copier goroutines block forever on the send out <- v, leaking. The unbuffered or full output channel has no reader, so those goroutines can never finish. The fix is to give each copier a way to abandon its work, typically by selecting on a context's Done channel alongside the input read and the output send, so cancelling the context unblocks them and lets them return. This is why the context-aware variant is the safer pattern for long-lived pipelines.

question: Implement a token-bucket rate limiter that allows a burst and refills at a steady rate.
thoughtProcess: A token bucket holds up to a capacity of tokens; each request consumes one, and tokens refill at a fixed rate over time. Rather than running a background ticker, I compute tokens lazily: on each Allow call I add tokens proportional to the elapsed time since the last refill, cap at capacity, and consume one if available. A mutex protects the shared token count and timestamp. This is the same model as golang.org/x/time/rate, which I would use in production, but implementing it shows the mechanism.
lineByLine: The bucket stores its capacity, current tokens as a float for fractional refills, the refill rate in tokens per second, and the last refill time, all guarded by a mutex. Allow locks, computes the seconds elapsed since last, and advances last to now. It adds elapsed times the rate worth of tokens, clamping to capacity so unused capacity does not accumulate beyond the burst limit. If at least one whole token is available it consumes one and allows the request, otherwise it denies it. Using floats lets tokens refill smoothly between calls without a background goroutine.

alternativeApproaches.title: golang.org/x/time/rate.Limiter
alternativeApproaches.explanation: The standard extended library provides a production-grade token bucket with Allow, Wait, and Reserve. Prefer it over a hand-rolled limiter in real code; the manual version is for demonstrating the mechanism.

alternativeApproaches.title: Ticker-based refill
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Run a background goroutine on a time.Ticker that adds a token periodically up to capacity. Conceptually simple but wastes a goroutine per limiter and refills in discrete steps rather than smoothly, and you still need a lock or channel for the token count.

followUps.question: Why compute tokens lazily on each call instead of using a background ticker?
followUps.answer: Lazy computation needs no extra goroutine: you derive the current token count from the elapsed time whenever Allow is called, which scales to thousands of limiters without thousands of background goroutines. It also refills smoothly and continuously rather than in discrete ticker steps, so timing is more precise. A ticker approach burns a goroutine and a timer per limiter and only adds tokens at the tick granularity. The lazy approach is exactly what golang.org/x/time/rate does internally, deriving available tokens from timestamps.

followUps.question: How does a token bucket differ from a leaky bucket or fixed window?
followUps.answer: A token bucket allows bursts up to its capacity, since saved-up tokens can be spent at once, while enforcing a steady average refill rate, which suits APIs that want to permit short spikes. A leaky bucket processes requests at a strictly constant rate, smoothing output and rejecting anything that overflows, so it does not allow bursts. A fixed-window counter resets a count every interval and is simple but suffers the boundary problem where twice the limit can pass across the edge of two adjacent windows. The token bucket's burst tolerance is its main distinguishing feature.

question: Implement a concurrency-safe counter, and show both a Mutex and an atomic version. When is each appropriate?
thoughtProcess: A counter incremented from many goroutines needs synchronization or it has a data race. Two idiomatic options: a sync.Mutex guarding a plain int, which generalizes to any compound operation, or sync/atomic operations on an int64, which are lock-free and faster for a single counter. I show both. The mutex is more flexible for multi-field updates; atomics are leaner for one value.
lineByLine: MutexCounter pairs a mutex with the count; Inc locks, increments, unlocks, so only one goroutine mutates n at a time, and Value reads under the lock to get a consistent snapshot. AtomicCounter uses the typed atomic.Int64 from the standard library; Add atomically increments and Load atomically reads, with no explicit lock. Both are safe to call from many goroutines concurrently; the atomic version avoids lock acquisition entirely by using hardware atomic instructions.
spaceComplexity: O(1) — a single integer plus, for the mutex version, the lock.

alternativeApproaches.title: Channel-owned counter
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Confine the count to a single goroutine that owns it and serve Inc and Value over channels. Idiomatic 'share by communicating' but heavier than a mutex or atomic for a simple counter; useful when the counter is part of a larger actor-style state machine.

alternativeApproaches.title: Sharded counter
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Keep per-shard counters padded to avoid false sharing and sum them on read. Reduces contention under extreme write concurrency at the cost of a more expensive read, used in very hot counters.

followUps.question: When should you choose atomics over a mutex?
followUps.answer: Atomics fit when you are protecting a single word-sized value with a simple operation like increment, load, or compare-and-swap, where they are lock-free and faster because they map to single hardware instructions. A mutex is the right choice when you need to update multiple fields together as one consistent unit, or perform a compound read-modify-write that spans more than one variable, because a mutex makes the whole critical section atomic while separate atomic operations do not. The rule of thumb is atomics for one independent value, a mutex for any invariant spanning multiple values.

followUps.question: Why is c.n++ a data race without synchronization?
followUps.answer: The increment is not a single atomic machine operation; it compiles to a read of the current value, an add, and a write back. If two goroutines run it concurrently, both can read the same old value, both add one, and both write back the same result, so one increment is lost. Beyond lost updates, concurrent unsynchronized access to the same memory with at least one writer is undefined behavior in Go's memory model and can corrupt the value or be reordered. A mutex or an atomic operation makes the read-modify-write indivisible, eliminating the race.

question: Implement a debounce function: it should call the wrapped function only after a quiet period with no new calls.
thoughtProcess: Debouncing collapses a rapid burst of calls into a single invocation that fires only after activity stops for a given duration. I use a time.Timer that I reset on every trigger, so each new call pushes the firing time later; the wrapped function runs only once the timer finally elapses without interruption. A mutex guards the timer because triggers can come from multiple goroutines. Resetting an existing timer rather than creating a new one each time is the clean approach.
lineByLine: Debouncer stores the quiet-period delay and the currently pending timer, guarded by a mutex. Trigger locks so concurrent triggers serialize. If a timer is already pending it stops it, cancelling the previously scheduled call, then schedules a fresh one with time.AfterFunc, which runs fn in its own goroutine after delay. Because each Trigger cancels the prior timer and starts a new one, fn only executes once the calls stop for a full delay, collapsing a burst into a single trailing invocation.
spaceComplexity: O(1) — one timer plus the lock.

alternativeApproaches.title: Throttle instead of debounce
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Throttling guarantees fn runs at most once per interval regardless of how many calls arrive, firing on a steady cadence rather than waiting for quiet. Use a token of elapsed time or a ticker; it suits rate-capping continuous events whereas debounce suits 'wait until input settles'.

alternativeApproaches.title: Channel-and-select debounce
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Run a goroutine that selects between an event channel and a timer; each event resets the timer, and the timer's fire triggers fn. More idiomatic for a long-lived pipeline but more code than AfterFunc for a simple debouncer.

followUps.question: What is the difference between debounce and throttle?
followUps.answer: Debounce waits for a quiet period: it fires the function only after calls stop for the configured duration, so a continuous stream of calls produces a single trailing invocation once activity ceases, which is ideal for things like search-as-you-type or resize handlers. Throttle enforces a maximum rate: it fires at most once per interval regardless of how many calls come in, producing a steady cadence during continuous activity, which suits scroll handlers or rate-capping. Debounce collapses bursts to one call after they end; throttle samples the stream at a fixed frequency while it continues.

followUps.question: Why guard the timer with a mutex?
followUps.answer: Trigger can be called from multiple goroutines, and it reads and writes the shared d.timer field by stopping the old timer and assigning a new one, which is a non-atomic compound operation. Without the lock, two concurrent triggers could race on the timer pointer, leaking a timer or losing the cancellation so the function fires more than intended, and the field access itself would be a data race flagged by the race detector. The mutex makes the stop-and-reschedule sequence atomic so the debouncer behaves correctly under concurrent triggers.

question: Implement generic Map, Filter, and Reduce functions using Go generics.
thoughtProcess: Go added type parameters in 1.18, so I can write Map, Filter, and Reduce once for any element type instead of per type. Map transforms each element to a possibly different type, so it needs two type parameters. Filter keeps elements matching a predicate, preserving the type. Reduce folds the slice into a single accumulator of a potentially different type, taking an initial value and a combining function. These are pure, allocation-clear functions over slices.
lineByLine: Map has type parameters T (input) and U (output), both any; it preallocates a result slice of len(s) and applies f to each element by index. Filter keeps the element type T and builds a result with capacity len(s) to avoid reallocation, appending only elements for which keep returns true. Reduce takes an initial accumulator of type U and a function combining the accumulator with each element; it folds left over the slice and returns the final accumulator, letting the result type differ from the element type, for example summing strings into an int length.
timeComplexity: O(n) for each — a single pass applying the supplied function per element.
spaceComplexity: Map and Filter O(n) for the result slice; Reduce O(1) beyond the accumulator.

alternativeApproaches.title: Standard library slices and maps packages
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Go 1.21+ ships slices and maps helpers, and slices.Collect plus iterators in 1.23 cover much of this. Prefer standard or well-maintained generic utility libraries over hand-rolled ones in production for consistency and testing.

alternativeApproaches.title: Constraint-based numeric generics
alternativeApproaches.explanation: For numeric operations you can constrain T with golang.org/x/exp/constraints (e.g. constraints.Ordered) so the function can use operators like + or < directly inside, rather than passing a combining function.

followUps.question: Why does Map need two type parameters while Filter needs only one?
followUps.answer: Map transforms each element into a value of a potentially different type, for example ints to strings, so it must name both the input type T and the output type U and return a []U. Filter only decides whether to keep each element and never changes its type, so the output slice is the same type T as the input and a single type parameter suffices. Reduce, like Map, can produce a different type from its elements, the accumulator type U, which is why it also carries two type parameters.

followUps.question: What are the tradeoffs of generics versus interface{} for these helpers?
followUps.answer: Before generics you would use interface{} and type assertions, which lose compile-time type safety, require boxing every value, and force the caller to assert types back, risking runtime panics. Generics give you type safety checked at compile time, no boxing for the common case, and a clean API where the compiler infers types from arguments. The tradeoffs are slightly longer compile times and that generic code is monomorphized or uses dictionaries under the hood, but for collection utilities like these the safety and ergonomics clearly favor generics over interface{}.

question: Build a bounded-concurrency web crawler that fetches a list of URLs with at most N concurrent requests, using errgroup.
thoughtProcess: I need bounded concurrency, error propagation, and cancellation. golang.org/x/sync/errgroup gives all three: errgroup.WithContext returns a group whose context is cancelled when any goroutine errors, and SetLimit bounds how many goroutines run at once. I launch one Go per URL, each fetching and storing its result under a mutex, and Wait returns the first error after cancelling the rest. This is cleaner and safer than hand-managing a semaphore plus a WaitGroup plus error collection.
lineByLine: errgroup.WithContext gives a group g and a derived ctx that is cancelled the moment any g.Go function returns an error. SetLimit caps the number of simultaneously running goroutines to limit, providing bounded concurrency without a manual semaphore. A mutex guards the shared sizes map. For each URL, g.Go runs a fetch: it builds a request bound to ctx so a cancellation aborts in-flight requests, performs it, reads and counts the body bytes via io.Copy to io.Discard, and records the size under the lock. g.Wait blocks until all goroutines finish or the first error surfaces, returning that error after the shared context has cancelled the others.
timeComplexity: O(number of URLs) requests, executed at most limit at a time.
spaceComplexity: O(number of URLs) for the results map plus O(limit) concurrent goroutines.

alternativeApproaches.title: Semaphore channel plus WaitGroup
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Bound concurrency with a buffered channel used as a semaphore (acquire by sending, release by receiving) and track completion with a WaitGroup, collecting errors manually. Works without errgroup but you must wire up cancellation and first-error logic yourself.

alternativeApproaches.title: Worker pool over a URL channel
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Start exactly limit workers that range over a channel of URLs. Fixed goroutine count rather than one per URL gated by a limiter; preferable when the URL set is huge so you never create a goroutine per URL even briefly.

followUps.question: How does SetLimit bound concurrency compared to a semaphore?
followUps.answer: SetLimit makes g.Go block when limit goroutines are already running, only starting the next one when a slot frees up, so it caps active concurrency internally just like a counting semaphore would. The difference is ergonomic: errgroup integrates the limit with its error propagation and shared context, so you get bounding, first-error capture, and cancellation in one tool. A raw semaphore channel does the same bounding but leaves you to combine it manually with a WaitGroup and your own error and cancellation handling, which is more code and easier to get subtly wrong.

followUps.question: Why bind the HTTP request to the errgroup context?
followUps.answer: errgroup.WithContext cancels its context as soon as any goroutine returns an error, and building each request with http.NewRequestWithContext means an in-flight HTTP call is aborted when that context is cancelled. So if one fetch fails, the others that are mid-request stop promptly instead of running to completion on work whose result will be discarded. Without binding the context, the goroutines would not see the cancellation during a blocking network call and would waste time and connections finishing requests for an already-failed batch.

question: Implement a producer-consumer pipeline that stops cleanly when a context is cancelled.
thoughtProcess: A producer pushes items onto a channel and a consumer reads them; both must respect context cancellation so the pipeline shuts down without leaking goroutines or blocking forever. The producer selects between sending the next item and ctx.Done, and closes the channel when it finishes or is cancelled. The consumer ranges over the channel, which ends when the producer closes it, and also watches ctx so it can stop promptly. Closing the channel from the producer side signals normal completion.
lineByLine: produce returns a channel and spawns a goroutine that defers close(out) so the channel is always closed on exit. Its loop selects between ctx.Done, on which it returns and triggers the deferred close, and sending the next value, so a blocked send cannot hang past cancellation. consume loops selecting on ctx.Done to bail early and on receiving from in; the comma-ok form detects the closed channel and returns the accumulated sum on normal completion. run wires producer to consumer, collects the total in a goroutine tracked by a WaitGroup, and returns once consumption finishes.
spaceComplexity: O(1) beyond the channel; the channel here is unbuffered.

alternativeApproaches.title: Buffered channel for throughput
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Give the channel a buffer so the producer can run ahead of a momentarily slow consumer, smoothing bursts. The cancellation logic is identical; the buffer only changes how much in-flight work can queue between the two.

alternativeApproaches.title: Multiple consumers (fan-out)
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Start several consumer goroutines ranging over the same channel to parallelize processing, with a WaitGroup to know when all finish. Use this when consumption is the bottleneck and the work per item is independent.

followUps.question: Why must the producer, not the consumer, close the channel?
followUps.answer: The Go convention is that the sender closes a channel, because closing signals that no more values will be sent, which only the sender can know. If a consumer closed it, the producer might still try to send and panic, since sending on a closed channel panics. With a single producer it defers close(out) so the channel closes exactly once when production ends or is cancelled, and consumers detect that via the comma-ok receive. With multiple producers you would coordinate with a WaitGroup and have a single goroutine close the channel after all producers finish.

followUps.question: Why does the producer select on ctx.Done in addition to the send?
followUps.answer: If the consumer stops reading, for instance because the context was cancelled, an unbuffered send out <- i blocks forever waiting for a receiver, leaking the producer goroutine. Selecting on ctx.Done alongside the send means cancellation unblocks the producer immediately so it can return and close the channel rather than hanging. This is the core idiom for cancellation-aware pipelines: every potentially blocking channel operation in a long-lived goroutine should be paired with a ctx.Done case so the goroutine always has an exit path.

question: Count the frequency of each word in a string, case-insensitively.
thoughtProcess: Word frequency counting is a classic map exercise. I normalize case with strings.ToLower, split on whitespace with strings.Fields (which handles runs of spaces and trims cleanly), and increment a map counter per word. Go maps return the zero value for missing keys, so I can increment directly without checking existence first. The result is a map from word to count.
lineByLine: freq is the result map from word to count. strings.ToLower normalizes the whole text so counting is case-insensitive. strings.Fields splits on any run of whitespace and discards empty tokens, so leading, trailing, and repeated spaces are handled without manual cleanup. For each resulting word, freq[w]++ increments its count; because a missing key reads as 0, the first occurrence of a word becomes 1 with no existence check needed. The populated map is returned.
timeComplexity: O(n) in the length of the text — one pass to lowercase and split, one to count.
spaceComplexity: O(k) where k is the number of distinct words.

alternativeApproaches.title: Manual scan with field separator function
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Use strings.FieldsFunc with a custom predicate to also split on punctuation, so 'word,' and 'word' count together. More accurate for natural text where punctuation should not be part of a word.

alternativeApproaches.title: bufio.Scanner with ScanWords
alternativeApproaches.explanation: For large or streamed input, a bufio.Scanner set to ScanWords reads word by word without loading the whole text into memory, which matters when the source is a file or network stream rather than a string.

followUps.question: How would you return the top K most frequent words?
followUps.answer: After building the frequency map, you collect the entries into a slice of word-count pairs and find the K largest counts. For small K relative to the number of words, a min-heap of size K is efficient at O(n log K); for a full ordering you sort the slice by count descending, O(n log n). For ties you typically add a secondary sort by the word itself for deterministic output. If K is close to the total, sorting is simplest; if K is tiny and the vocabulary huge, the heap avoids sorting everything.

followUps.question: Why does strings.Fields handle whitespace better than strings.Split?
followUps.answer: strings.Split(text, " ") splits on each single space, so multiple consecutive spaces, tabs, or newlines produce empty strings in the result that you would then have to filter out, and it does not treat tabs or newlines as separators at all. strings.Fields splits on any run of Unicode whitespace and never yields empty tokens, so leading, trailing, and repeated whitespace and mixed whitespace characters are all handled correctly with no post-processing. For tokenizing words it is the right primitive precisely because it collapses arbitrary whitespace cleanly.

question: Detect whether a directed graph contains a cycle, using DFS with node coloring.
thoughtProcess: Cycle detection in a directed graph uses DFS with three states per node: unvisited (white), in the current recursion stack (gray), and fully explored (black). If during DFS I reach a node that is currently gray, I have found a back edge, which means a cycle. A node turning black means its whole subtree is cycle-free. I represent the graph as an adjacency list and track state in a slice.
lineByLine: The color constants encode the three DFS states. color tracks each of the n nodes, all starting white. The recursive dfs marks the current node gray to put it on the active path, then visits each neighbor: a gray neighbor is a back edge into the current path, proving a cycle, so it returns true; a white neighbor is explored recursively. After all neighbors are done with no cycle found, the node is marked black, fully explored. The outer loop starts a DFS from every still-white node so disconnected components are all covered, returning true if any DFS finds a cycle.
timeComplexity: O(V + E) — each vertex and edge is examined once.
spaceComplexity: O(V) for the color slice plus up to O(V) recursion depth.

alternativeApproaches.title: Kahn's algorithm (topological sort)
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Repeatedly remove nodes with in-degree zero; if you cannot remove all nodes, the remaining ones form a cycle. Iterative rather than recursive, avoiding deep-recursion stack limits, and it also yields a topological order when acyclic.
alternativeApproaches.code:
// process nodes with indegree 0 via a queue;
// if processed count < n, a cycle exists

alternativeApproaches.title: Iterative DFS with an explicit stack
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Replace recursion with an explicit stack carrying node and child-iterator state, marking gray on push and black on full pop. Useful for very deep graphs where recursion would overflow the goroutine stack.

followUps.question: Why does cycle detection in a directed graph need three colors, while an undirected graph needs only two?
followUps.answer: In a directed graph, simply revisiting an already-visited node does not imply a cycle, because it might be a fully-explored node reachable by another path, a cross or forward edge. You need the gray state to distinguish nodes currently on the active recursion path, since only an edge back to a gray node is a true back edge forming a cycle. In an undirected graph, two colors suffice: any edge to a visited node other than the immediate parent is a cycle, so you track visited plus the parent rather than needing the gray/black distinction.

followUps.question: When would you prefer Kahn's algorithm over DFS coloring?
followUps.answer: Kahn's algorithm is iterative and queue-based, so it avoids the deep-recursion stack growth that DFS coloring incurs on long paths, which matters for very large or deep graphs where recursion could overflow the goroutine stack. It also naturally produces a topological ordering as a byproduct when the graph is acyclic, so if you need both the acyclicity check and an order, Kahn's gives both in one pass. DFS coloring is often more concise and is preferable when you only need a yes/no cycle answer and the graph depth is bounded.

question: Merge a slice of intervals, combining any that overlap.
thoughtProcess: The standard approach is to sort the intervals by start, then sweep through merging. After sorting, I walk the list keeping the current merged interval; if the next interval starts at or before the current end, they overlap so I extend the current end to the max of the two; otherwise there is a gap, so I push the current interval and start a new one. Sorting dominates the cost at O(n log n).
lineByLine: An empty input returns nil early. sort.Slice orders intervals ascending by their start value so overlaps become adjacent. merged is seeded with the first interval. For each subsequent interval cur, last is the most recently merged interval; if cur starts at or before last's end they overlap, so last's end is extended to the larger end (covering the case where cur is fully contained, where the end stays). If cur starts after last's end there is a gap, so cur begins a new merged interval appended to the result. The merged list is returned.
timeComplexity: O(n log n) — dominated by the sort; the merge sweep is O(n).
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the output (O(1) extra if sorting in place and ignoring output).

alternativeApproaches.title: Sort by start and end events (sweep line)
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Treat each start as +1 and each end as -1, sort all events, and sweep tracking active count; a merged interval spans from when the count rises above zero to when it returns to zero. Generalizes nicely to counting overlaps, not just merging.

alternativeApproaches.title: Define an Interval struct
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Use a struct with named Start and End fields instead of [][]int for clarity and type safety, sorting a []Interval. Cleaner API in real code; the [][]int form matches common interview phrasing.
alternativeApproaches.code:
type Interval struct{ Start, End int }
sort.Slice(iv, func(i, j int) bool { return iv[i].Start < iv[j].Start })

followUps.question: Why is sorting by start the key step that makes the linear merge correct?
followUps.answer: Once intervals are sorted by start, any interval that could overlap the current merged interval must come immediately after it, because all later intervals start at or after the current one's start. So a single left-to-right pass suffices: you only ever need to compare the next interval against the most recently merged one, never against earlier ones, since those have smaller or equal starts and are already accounted for. Without sorting, overlaps could be scattered anywhere in the input, forcing an O(n^2) all-pairs comparison instead of the O(n) sweep.

followUps.question: How do you handle intervals that merely touch, like [1,2] and [2,3]?
followUps.answer: Whether touching intervals merge depends on the definition. The code uses cur[0] <= last[1], so [1,2] and [2,3] merge into [1,3], treating a shared endpoint as overlapping, which is the common convention for closed intervals. If touching intervals should stay separate, for example when endpoints are exclusive, you change the comparison to a strict cur[0] < last[1] so only a genuine overlap merges them. The single character difference encodes the interval semantics, so you clarify the intended convention before choosing it.

question: Implement an HTTP middleware chain: a Chain helper that composes multiple middleware around a final http.Handler, plus example logging and auth middleware.
thoughtProcess: Standard net/http middleware is a function that takes an http.Handler and returns a wrapping http.Handler, adding behavior before and after calling the wrapped handler. To compose several I write a Chain helper that applies them so the first one listed is outermost, which is the intuitive order. The trick is to wrap in reverse: iterate the middleware slice from last to first so the earliest-listed ends up on the outside. Each middleware is independent and testable, and the pattern is exactly what frameworks build on.
lineByLine: Middleware is a named type for the func(http.Handler) http.Handler shape so signatures read clearly. Chain wraps the handler by iterating the middleware slice from the last element to the first, so mws[0] is applied last and therefore sits outermost, giving the intuitive left-to-right ordering where the first listed runs first. Logging wraps a statusWriter around the ResponseWriter to capture the status code, records the start time, calls the inner handler via ServeHTTP, then logs method, path, captured status, and elapsed duration after it returns, demonstrating pre and post processing. Auth checks for an Authorization header and short-circuits with 401 by returning before calling next, otherwise it passes control inward. statusWriter embeds http.ResponseWriter and overrides WriteHeader to remember the code while still writing it through. main composes Logging and Auth around a trivial handler so every request is logged and gated.
timeComplexity: O(m) to build the chain for m middleware; O(1) per-request overhead per middleware layer.
spaceComplexity: O(m) nested handler wrappers plus O(1) per request for the status writer.

alternativeApproaches.title: Forward-fold with a reversed intent
alternativeApproaches.explanation: You could iterate the slice forward, but then the first-listed middleware becomes innermost, which is counterintuitive. Reversing the iteration (or reversing the slice) so the first listed is outermost matches how developers expect ordering to read, which is why the loop counts down.

alternativeApproaches.title: Use a router or framework middleware
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Routers like chi, gorilla/mux, or frameworks like Gin and Echo provide their own middleware chaining with per-route groups and richer context. In real services you usually use those rather than a hand-rolled Chain, but implementing Chain shows you understand what they do underneath.
alternativeApproaches.code:
r := chi.NewRouter()
r.Use(Logging, Auth)
r.Get("/", finalHandler)

followUps.question: Why does Chain iterate the middleware slice in reverse?
followUps.answer: Because wrapping is applied from the inside out: each call mws[i](h) makes mws[i] the new outermost layer around the current h. If you want the first middleware listed, mws[0], to be the outermost, the one that runs first on the way in and last on the way out, it must be applied last. Iterating from the last index down to zero applies mws[len-1] first (innermost) and mws[0] last (outermost), producing the intuitive order where Chain(h, Logging, Auth) runs Logging, then Auth, then the handler. Iterating forward instead would invert that, making the first-listed middleware innermost, which surprises callers. Reversing keeps the API's ordering match the reading order.

followUps.question: Why is a statusWriter wrapper needed to log the response status code?
followUps.answer: The standard http.ResponseWriter does not expose the status code that a handler wrote, and by the time the logging middleware regains control after next.ServeHTTP returns, the status has already been sent but is not readable from the writer. To capture it, you wrap the ResponseWriter in a type that embeds it and overrides WriteHeader to record the code before delegating to the real writer, so after the handler runs the middleware can read the captured status. If the handler never calls WriteHeader explicitly, the status defaults to 200, so you initialize the wrapper's status to http.StatusOK to reflect that. This wrapping is the standard technique any real access-logging or metrics middleware uses, and the same wrapper can also count bytes written.

question: Implement a concurrency-safe token-bucket rate limiter with a lazy refill and a per-client limiter registry.
thoughtProcess: A token bucket holds up to a capacity of tokens, each request consumes one, and tokens refill at a steady rate. I compute tokens lazily from elapsed time on each Allow call rather than running a background ticker, clamping to capacity so bursts are bounded, and guard the state with a mutex. To rate-limit per client rather than globally, I add a registry that maps a client key to its own bucket, protected by its own mutex, creating a bucket on first use. This mirrors how golang.org/x/time/rate is used per key in production, which I would prefer in real code.
lineByLine: TokenBucket stores capacity, current tokens as a float for fractional refills, the refill rate per second, and the last refill time, all guarded by a mutex. Allow locks, adds tokens proportional to the seconds elapsed since last, clamps to capacity so unused capacity does not accumulate beyond the burst, advances last, and consumes one token if at least one is available, returning whether the request is allowed. The Limiter holds a map from a client key to that client's bucket plus the shared capacity and rate. Its Allow locks the registry only long enough to look up or lazily create the client's bucket, unlocks, then calls that bucket's own Allow, so per-client buckets do not contend on the registry lock during the actual rate check. Creating on first use means new clients get a full bucket.
timeComplexity: O(1) per Allow call, including the map lookup.
spaceComplexity: O(k) for k distinct client keys, each holding a constant-size bucket.

alternativeApproaches.title: golang.org/x/time/rate per key
alternativeApproaches.explanation: The standard extended library provides a production-grade token bucket. The common production pattern is a map of *rate.Limiter keyed by client, exactly like this registry, and you would use it rather than hand-rolling the bucket; the manual version demonstrates the mechanism.

alternativeApproaches.title: Distributed limiting with Redis
alternativeApproaches.explanation: An in-memory registry limits per instance, so across a fleet the effective limit is multiplied by instance count. For a global limit you move the token accounting into Redis, typically with an atomic Lua script implementing the bucket, so all instances share one counter per key at the cost of a network round trip.

followUps.question: Why compute tokens lazily on each call instead of refilling with a background goroutine?
followUps.answer: Lazy computation derives the current token count from the elapsed time whenever Allow is called, so it needs no background goroutine per bucket, which matters enormously when you have one bucket per client and potentially thousands of clients, since a goroutine and timer each would be wasteful and would not scale. It also refills continuously and precisely rather than in discrete ticker steps, so timing is smoother and there is no drift between ticks. A background-ticker approach burns a goroutine and timer per limiter and only adds tokens at the tick granularity, and you still need synchronization on the count. The lazy approach is exactly what golang.org/x/time/rate does internally, deriving available tokens from timestamps, which is why it is the standard technique.

followUps.question: The registry map grows unbounded as new client keys appear; how would you address that in production?
followUps.answer: Because the registry creates a bucket per key and never removes them, a service that sees many distinct clients over time, especially with attacker-controlled or high-cardinality keys, will leak memory as the map grows without bound. In production you add eviction: track a last-seen time per bucket and run a periodic sweeper goroutine that removes buckets idle beyond a threshold, since an idle bucket refills to full anyway so recreating it loses nothing; or you bound the map with an LRU cache that evicts the least-recently-used entries when it reaches a size cap. You would also guard the key space itself, for example limiting by a bounded attribute like a hashed IP or an authenticated account rather than an arbitrary client-supplied string, so the cardinality is controlled. The cleanup must itself be concurrency-safe, taking the registry lock while deleting entries.
